_about: Claims register for the FabCon Europe 2026 debrief. Every statement on the site must trace to a claim here. Do not publish a claim without its evidence label.

_evidence_labels.slide: The statement is on a slide that the attendee holds as a deck or a photo. It is the speaker's statement, not a tested fact.
_evidence_labels.notes: The statement is in the attendee's handwritten session notes only. No slide is held.
_evidence_labels.docs: The statement is in Microsoft documentation or a Microsoft blog, found on 2026-10-04.
_evidence_labels.third-party: The statement is from an independent article or a vendor. Treat it with care.
_evidence_labels.research: The statement is from an academic paper.
_evidence_labels.inference: The attendee or the assistant made this conclusion from the other evidence. It is not a source statement.

_rule: Speaker statements about their own demos keep the speaker's own limits (for example 'customer reported', 'fictional workload', 'design only'). Keep the 'caveat' text when you use the claim.

claims.text: The keynote put customer context at the centre. The slide showed 'Your IQ' above 'Microsoft IQ', above Foundry, Azure and Fabric. Copilot and Agent 365 were at the sides.
claims.caveat: The spoken line was 'you've spent years building knowledge about your business ... it's your competitive advantage, it's your context' (live caption, IMG_2647).

claims.text: Microsoft IQ has four parts: Work IQ, Foundry IQ, Fabric IQ and Web IQ.

sources.loc: attendee notes: 'Microsoft IQ - work, foundry, fabric, web'

claims.text: The ontology item in Fabric IQ holds business entities and their relationships. You bind each entity to data in OneLake. The ontology is not a query engine. Agents use it as context and run each query against the bound data source.
claims.caveat: Microsoft Learn changed this description on 1 October 2026. Earlier sources said that the ontology sends each query to an engine.

claims.text: Keep measures in the semantic model. Add an ontology when agents must navigate related concepts.
claims.caveat: This is the speaker's design rule.

claims.text: Fabric can generate an ontology from a Power BI semantic model. Tables become entities and relationships become connections.

On 18 September 2026, the ontology preview had these limits in Microsoft Learn. The graph refresh was manual. A user needed the Workspace Contributor role, not Viewer. Row-level security through bindings was not documented.
claims.caveat: The speaker read these limits from Microsoft Learn on 18 September 2026. Learn changed on 1 October 2026. It now says that querying respects OneLake security and row-level security at the source, and that the graph is optional. We did not test this.

claims.text: 'Prep data for AI' lets a model author set an AI data schema, verified answers and AI instructions. The 'Approved for Copilot' setting removes the warning that Copilot shows for unprepared models.

sources.loc: attendee notes: 'Prep semantic model for AI', 'Toggle in Fabric approve for copilot'

claims.caveat: The setting was named 'prepped for AI' before.

claims.text: Microsoft announced Fabric IQ as generally available at Build 2026. The ontology item stayed in preview. Microsoft Learn still showed a preview label on the workload in September 2026.

sources.loc: slide 10 kicker: 'Fabric IQ (preview workload) - ontology is a separate preview item'

claims.caveat: Sources disagree on the label. Use 'ontology: preview' and do not state a status for the full workload without a new check.

claims.text: Microsoft describes data agents as 'context engineering for shared curated views of data and knowledge for a purpose'. Data agents can reason across ontologies and graph models, not only tables.
People teach the system the business. Frontline knowledge becomes data definitions, then a semantic model. Each translation removes some context.
The agent sees the model. The agent cannot see what the model excludes, such as exceptions and dissent.
AI-ready data makes assumptions executable. A report shows. An agent recommends. A system acts. What once shaped a dashboard can now shape a decision.
Readiness is organizational work. It needs shared definitions, access rules, exceptions, context and people who notice.
In the ontology demo, each entity type had a description field. The field text said that the description gives AI agents better context for how the entity type is used.
claims.caveat: Read from a photo of a live demo screen. Small text.

claims.text: The ontology session said that an ontology makes sense only for the business context, and that governance policies should enable work.
claims.caveat: No slide is held for this statement.

claims.text: Each connector route to a Fabric data agent has a different identity contract. Foundry data agent tool: runs as the signed-in user (on-behalf-of), preview. Foundry Fabric IQ tool: delegated user, preview. Copilot Studio Fabric IQ Data MCP tool: user or maker credentials, generally available. Direct MCP client: user token or service-principal token, with service-principal access in preview.

sources.loc: slide 13, source checks 15-17 Sep 2026, status 23-25 Sep

claims.caveat: Only the Copilot Studio route was demonstrated. The other rows are from documentation that the speaker checked.

claims.text: The credential mode decides whose data the agent sees. 'Maker' uses the builder's credentials. 'User' uses the credentials of the person who asks. The settings pane shows a choice. It is not proof of the caller.
In the speaker's demo, 4 of 4 answers matched the reference figure. The caller was established at Fabric in 0 of 4.
claims.caveat: Synthetic data in the speaker's own tenant. The speaker states that no accuracy rate comes from four answers.

claims.text: On 24 September, a reader with access to one region asked about London and received London's figure. The route used maker credentials. The log named the maker's account.
claims.caveat: Speaker's demo, synthetic data.

claims.text: In the speaker's enterprise case, facts and tools used different identities. Questions to the semantic model ran on behalf of the user, so row-level security applied. A tool call ran as a service principal, so row-level security did not apply.
claims.caveat: The speaker marks this 'customer reported, not inspected'.

claims.text: Row-level security in a semantic model binds Viewers and read-only users. Editors are exempt. SQL and OneLake use separate permissions.
To prove the caller, read the semantic model operation log. The ExecutingUser field must name each reader account.
claims.caveat: Workspace logging was in preview in the speaker's tenant on 17 September 2026.

claims.text: The Fabric data agent tool in Foundry supports user identity only. An independent article says that service-principal authentication is not supported for that tool, and that unattended work must go to the data sources directly.
claims.caveat: Different from the direct MCP route in C201, where service-principal access is in preview. A Microsoft slide lists 'SPN support ... in Foundry' for data agents (S-PURVIEW-DATA, IMG_2685). The sources do not agree.

claims.text: Microsoft Entra Agent ID gives an agent its own identity. The identity is a special service principal made from a blueprint. A human sponsor can request access for the agent. Copilot Studio makes an agent identity for each new agent.
The governance session named Entra Agent ID with scoped, least-privilege access as the control for 'agents are a new identity to govern'.
claims.caveat: One line on one slide. No session showed how to use Agent ID with Fabric.

claims.text: Eligibility is not access. In a Privileged Identity Management test, the same request was denied before activation, allowed during activation and denied after.
claims.caveat: Controlled lab with an Azure Reader role. It does not prove Fabric row-level security.

claims.text: A tenant is one of five isolation controls. The others are identity, connectors, network and geography. Each needs its own test.
claims.caveat: The slide says that Private Link is not supported for semantic models and workspace monitoring 'currently'.

claims.text: A Fabric engine reaches OneLake in one of two modes. In passthrough mode, the engine reads data as the user. In delegated mode, the engine reads data as its own fixed identity, and the engine must apply its own security to tell users apart.

sources.loc: slides 'Engine Integration - Passthrough Mode' and 'Delegated Mode'

claims.text: No session showed how to give an unattended agent a narrow identity in Fabric.
claims.caveat: Open question.

claims.text: Access in Fabric can come from six layers: identity, workspace, item, data, inheritance and relationships. A permission is not the same as effective access.
Security is a graph, not a list. A user can reach the same data through different paths.
There is no single source of truth for the complete Fabric security picture. You must collect it from the Fabric REST APIs, the Power BI REST APIs, the OneLake APIs and the Microsoft Graph APIs.
Start with Microsoft Graph. Collect users, service principals, managed identities, groups and group members. Flatten nested groups so that each user links to each group.
The Fabric admin APIs list workspaces, items and workspace access. The item-access and OneLake-role endpoints are limited to 200 requests each hour.
claims.caveat: The tenant-level endpoints need Fabric admin rights.

claims.text: The speaker's method has five steps: capture, normalize, relate, query, explain. A Fabric data agent then answers questions such as 'Why can Alice see this?'
A OneLake security role has three parts: who (members), what (permission) and target (schema, table, column, row or folder). A user in more than one role gets the union of the roles.
Workspace Admins, Members and Contributors can read all data in OneLake. Only Viewers get their data access from OneLake security roles.
claims.caveat: The roadmap lists 'Restrict Admin/Member/Contributor access' as committed. Microsoft Learn gives one exception: in the user's identity mode of the SQL analytics endpoint, row-level security applies to all users, including these roles.

claims.text: A passthrough shortcut checks the user at the target. A delegated shortcut reads the target with a fixed identity, and then the consumer roles narrow the result. Consumer roles can narrow access. They cannot widen it.
claims.caveat: The slide gives the rule as A ∩ (C ∪ D).

claims.text: Shortcuts to external storage, such as S3 or ADLS Gen2, always use a delegated identity. Delegated OneLake shortcuts also work across tenants.
A new permissions view in OneLake answers 'Who has access to this table?' and 'What data can this user see?'
claims.caveat: The slide showed OneLake security roles only. Our reading: the view does not show semantic model security or access through groups.

claims.text: OneLake security is generally available. It filters data for Lakehouse, Spark notebooks, the SQL analytics endpoint, semantic models and Fabric Graph. Eventhouse and external engines are in preview.
claims.caveat: Microsoft Learn lists the same status for each engine. For semantic models, Learn names Direct Lake on OneLake mode. For the SQL analytics endpoint, Learn names the user's identity access mode.

claims.text: Column-level security removes hidden columns in Spark and Power BI. In SQL, the query must leave out the hidden columns. Data masking is not available.

sources.loc: slide 'Column level security'; roadmap lists data masking as 'Exploring'

claims.text: Column metadata will become searchable in the OneLake catalog by default. A user with Read permission on an item will see its table names, column names and descriptions. A tenant setting controls this.
The choice of engine is a security decision. An independent article says that Direct Lake over SQL and the SQL endpoint in delegated mode do not pass the user identity to OneLake.
claims.caveat: Check against Microsoft Learn before you rely on it.

claims.text: SQL injection and prompt injection use the same fault. The system does not separate code from data.
There is no 'sanitized' natural language. Instructions and untrusted data go through the same channel, so the model cannot fully separate them.
Prompt injection is number 1 in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications (2025). SQL injection is CWE-89, with about 13,900 CVEs.

For SQL injection, parameterised queries are the primary defence. Input validation and a web application firewall are additions, not replacements. Least-privilege database accounts limit all types of attack.

Prompt injection has five attack types: direct, indirect (hidden in documents, web pages or retrieved content), obfuscated, agent and multimodal, and amplified by many attempts. Attackers combine them.

For prompt injection, the slide lists 9 defences. Never execute model output directly. Separate trusted instructions, user data and tool output. Use approved, parameterised actions. Authorize each action on the server. Validate input. Give least privilege. Validate output. Monitor. Run agents in a sandbox.
claims.caveat: 'Limit what the agent can do' is our summary of this list.

claims.text: GitHub Copilot agent mode in SQL Server Management Studio uses a local MCP server with a predefined set of tools. You can add tools with MCP servers and agent skills. Queries run as the user, or as a database user that the CONSTITUTION.md file of the database names.

sources.loc: attendee notes: 'Database constitution and db instructions'

claims.caveat: Microsoft said on 29 September 2026 that agent mode is generally available.

claims.text: All users are a source of attack surface. Do not trust input, from AI or not.
The session's test for AI-ready data: 'Can you explain what data AI used, whether it was allowed, and what happened next?' AI-ready data is identified, authorized, protected and observable.
Gate each answer before it reaches the user. The speaker's five gates are meaning, access, retrieval, calculation and response. Each gate records a decision and a reason.
claims.caveat: A design. The speaker tested it in a local simulation, not on a Microsoft workload. The product enforces only the access gate.

claims.text: Rules validate figures. Models review wording. A model judge cannot prove arithmetic or identity.

'Resolved' is not a correct answer. In Copilot Studio, AI assigns the 'Resolved implied' outcome after the session ends. In the speaker's capture, the session was 'Resolved' and the reader got no figures.

Foundry documents one trace for each turn: the agent run, the tool call and the model call. Copilot Studio has no documented join between a chat turn and the Fabric query, so you must design the identifier in.
claims.caveat: Foundry tracing was generally available for prompt and hosted agents; Trace Replay was in preview (verified by the speaker 17 Sep 2026).

claims.text: Keep an evidence record for each answer. When a prompt, tool, model or permission changes, repeat the same question, and repeat the test with two readers who have different access.

Purview DSPM for AI can record prompts and responses for Fabric data agents and Copilot in Fabric. You must turn on Purview Audit, a collection policy and a Fabric tenant setting. Without the policy, Purview records the event but not the prompt and response.
claims.caveat: Microsoft Learn now names this version 'DSPM for AI (classic)' and says that a new version of Data Security Posture Management replaces it.

claims.text: Insider Risk Management for Fabric is generally available. It reads Fabric audit logs with other signals to find malicious or accidental activity. It is billed pay-as-you-go and needs a separate Purview purchase.
'100% approved' counts clicks. It does not show that the reviewer had time, evidence or authority. A click is easy to count. Judgment is harder.
A metric needs an obligation: alert, owner, threshold, action, review. An alert without an obligation is decoration.
Contestability needs infrastructure: decision, pause, appeal, review, change. The question is whether disagreement can change the outcome.
An isolation claim needs an allowed test and a denied test. Configure the control, test both, keep the evidence and name the gap.
A release is a version, its checks, an owner and a rehearsed recovery.
Three sessions ask for the same thing in different words: evidence of what the agent did. Permission alone is not enough.
claims.caveat: Synthesis by the attendee and the assistant.

claims.text: The governance session paired eight AI risks with eight controls. Oversharing: domains, item permissions, row and column security, access review. Bad data: Prep for AI, endorsed items, lineage. Regulatory exposure: Purview audit, sensitivity labels, automatic classification. Trust: Approved for Copilot, lineage and Git history. Agents as a new identity: Entra Agent ID. Accountability: Git, pull requests, human review. Speed against control: self-service inside domain guardrails. Shadow AI: one governed mono-repo for context, MCP servers and skills.
The session split AI use into two modes. Conversational analytics: Copilot and agents on business data. Agentic development: LLMs, MCP servers, skills, tools and command-line tools.

The session showed four AI maturity steps: manual development, chat assisted, agent-assisted development and autonomous AI teams. Step 3 needs organization-wide context and governance. Step 2 has no shared context.

For scale, keep one governed source of truth for what agents know and can do. One mono-repo holds shared context, MCP servers and skills. Development agents use it. Each change goes through a pull request with human review.
A governance agent can review the Fabric tenant and propose fixes as pull requests. A human reviews each one before it reaches development, test or production.
claims.caveat: Shown as a live demo. The demo used a tool named 'onelake-catalog-govern-cli'.

claims.text: Fabric Atlas is a community tool by Frederic Gisbert. It gives one view of the catalog, lineage, governance, access and operations of a Fabric workspace. It stores metadata only.
claims.caveat: A community accelerator, not a Microsoft product.

claims.text: Domains give real ownership. Self-service happens in the workspace, inside domain guardrails. Workspaces connect to Git.
Start with sensitivity labels. Set a default label at the domain level. Make labels mandatory on save. Use programmatic labelling to start. Labels pass to downstream items.

sources.loc: photo IMG_2711; attendee notes: 'Keep it small but specific', 'Default label as internal'

claims.text: Purview data loss prevention can now restrict access to a Fabric item when a rule matches. The steps are detect, contain, investigate, resolve.
claims.caveat: The slide did not show a status label.

claims.text: Some controls are built into Fabric: the Govern tab, OneLake security, domains, endorsement, lineage and monitoring. Sensitivity labels, data loss prevention, audit, insider risk and DSPM for AI need a Microsoft Purview licence.

Purview has five tools for data security: information protection, data loss prevention, audit, insider risk management and data security posture management. They work across the full Microsoft estate, not only Fabric.
The Govern tab in the OneLake catalog shows governance insights and recommended actions. It works without Purview. Its tenant-wide semantic model is read-only, and a Fabric data agent cannot use it.
Research on agent-written code is mixed. One study found more corrective maintenance and more security weaknesses than in human code. A different study found fewer security smells.
claims.caveat: Two preprints. Use them to show that a human review gate needs design, not to rank agents.

claims.text: The last line of the attendee's notes for this session: architecture and governance are what will make AI work.
Teams expect 70% of the effort in an LLM project to be the prototype. The actual split is 10% prototype, 30% evaluation, 40% data preparation and RAG, and 20% infrastructure.
claims.caveat: The speaker's estimate. The slide gives no data source.

claims.text: Applications must talk to an AI gateway, not to a model directly. The gateway gives model routing, cost tracking, token logging, access control, one API standard, and governance and audit. Models become replaceable.
claims.caveat: The slide names LiteLLM as the example.

claims.text: An agent can loop on a failed tool call and spend money each time. Use budget guards, rate limits for each session, and cost alerts.
Most RAG failures happen at the retrieval stage. RAG latency is one of the biggest adoption killers in the enterprise. You must have a method to find vector data that is out of sync with the source.

Responsible AI has three layers: operational governance (gateways, logging, cost), platform governance (safety filters, evaluations, guardrails) and organizational governance (policies, approvals, accountability, human in the loop).
You pay for each attempt, not for each answer. In the speaker's fictional workload, a useful answer cost about GBP 0.15 on Fabric capacity and about GBP 0.064 on a customer model deployment.
claims.caveat: Fictional workload. Fabric capacity is at the one-year reservation rate for UK South. Other lines are at public list prices of 15 September 2026. Copilot credits were unknown and not included. The second figure does not include Fabric capacity for the data. Do not present these as real costs.

claims.text: Fabric smooths AI work across 24 hours. Queries that the agent generates are interactive, and they throttle first. Throttling starts as a 20-second delay.
claims.caveat: Default policy from Microsoft Learn, verified by the speaker 17 Sep 2026.

claims.text: The speaker's advice for AI development: walk before you run, control the prompts, put technical guardrails in place, have a plan for data poisoning, set a caching strategy, and plan for generated data.
Technology that works is not enough. If back-end costs grow faster than the time saved, the result is a net loss. The slide gave agentic workloads as 5 to 30 times more tokens.
claims.caveat: No data source on the slide.

claims.text: The Purview session opened with adoption and risk statistics. Their sources are dated 2023 and 2024.
claims.caveat: Do not quote these numbers as current.

claims.text: Both things are true. OneLake gives less fragmentation and more data gravity. Semantic models give shared meaning and fixed assumptions. Copilots give wider access and assumptions at scale. Integrated governance gives more visibility and more control. Benefits and concentration can grow together.
claims.caveat: This slide was shown in the session and is in the attendee's photo. It is not in the 70-slide deck that the speaker shared.

claims.text: Six questions test what you can still choose. Can we export data, definitions and history? Does knowledge exist outside one vendor interface? Can people challenge a metric or an automated decision? Are model assumptions documented? Who receives the time supposedly saved? Can someone refuse without paying a career penalty?
claims.caveat: In the attendee's photo, not in the shared deck.

claims.text: Usefulness can become dependency: useful, adopt, depend, lock-in.
When the vendor changes the model, ask two questions. Is there a change log? Who noticed?
The keynote showed many engines that can read OneLake data, such as Databricks, Snowflake, Spark, Trino and DuckDB. The OneLake session showed one copy of the data for all compute engines.
claims.caveat: Our reading: this is how Microsoft answers the lock-in question. Open data formats do not make ontologies, AI instructions or agent definitions portable. No session that we attended covered export of those.

claims.text: OneLake security has APIs that let any engine read and enforce its rules. Microsoft plans open-source security interoperability.

sources.loc: slides 'V2: Any Engine can Integrate', 'OneLake security - roadmap'

claims.text: The keynote showed a 'Sovereign Private Cloud': Foundry Local, data platform services and customer applications on Azure Local.
No session showed how Purview covers a custom agent that is built outside Foundry and Copilot Studio.

sources.loc: photo IMG_2679 lists supported AI apps

claims.caveat: Open question. W30 is from a vendor with a competing product.

claims.text: Azure SQL Database: vector compression and a live vector index with full insert, update and delete support.
claims.caveat: Microsoft Learn says that index maintenance runs in the background.

claims.text: Database agents: detect, understand, verify, learn, automate. They work across Azure SQL, SQL Server, Azure HorizonDB and Azure Database for PostgreSQL, with skills, tools and connectors.
claims.caveat: Microsoft said on 28 September 2026 that database agents for SQL and PostgreSQL on Azure 'will soon be available in preview'. That text does not name Azure HorizonDB.

claims.text: SQL developer tools: Copilot chat in SQL Server Management Studio, vector and JSON data in Data API builder, Schema Compare and SQL Projects in SSMS, and a SQL formatter.

A new certification: SQL AI Developer Associate (DP-800). It covers AI-augmented SQL development, AI-first applications, and security, governance and responsible AI. Conference attendees get a free exam and three vouchers to share.
claims.caveat: The slide gave no expiry date. We did not confirm the release date of the exam.

claims.text: Microsoft acquired Osmos in January 2026. Its technology is now a data engineering agent in Fabric, announced in preview at this conference.
OneLake Table Read API: an agent or application reads a Delta or Iceberg table without SQL. OneLake applies table, column and row security on each read and returns Apache Arrow.

sources.loc: slides 'Announcing: OneLake Table Read API', 'Table Read API - Step 1'

claims.caveat: Billing is by rows scanned.

claims.text: Dynamic and multi-table row-level security in OneLake: rules can use the name of the user and can join other tables. Estimated for the first quarter of 2027.

sources.loc: slides 'Fabcon exclusive sneak peak', 'Dynamic RLS - New Predicates'

claims.caveat: Marked 'NOT available yet'.

claims.text: Fabric data agents are generally available. Operations agents monitor real-time data and act.

sources.loc: attendee notes: 'Fabric has two agents: operations and data'

claims.text: The Database Hub in Fabric gives one view of databases across edge, cloud and Fabric. It is agent-assisted, with a human in the loop.

sources.loc: attendee notes: 'Database hub - fleet management, observability'

claims.text: Fabric IQ in Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and Cowork is generally available. Fabric IQ context also reaches agents in Foundry, Copilot Studio and MCP clients.
claims.caveat: The 'generally available' statement is for Copilot Chat and Cowork only (Microsoft, 28 September 2026). We did not confirm the status of the other routes.

claims.text: Automatic index compaction removes the need for scheduled index maintenance jobs.
claims.caveat: Microsoft said on 29 September 2026 that it is generally available.

claims.text: The keynote covered AI-guided, policy-based governance in the OneLake catalog, and mirroring of SharePoint and OneDrive.
claims.caveat: No slide is held. Not confirmed in documentation.

claims.text: A Microsoft executive said at the conference: 'Fabric is becoming the center point for everything data at Microsoft and everything that's context based on data.'
claims.caveat: Press report of a spoken statement.

claims.text: How does an ontology apply row-level security? On 18 September 2026, the preview documentation did not say. Since 1 October 2026, Microsoft Learn says that authoring and querying respect row-level security at the source. We did not test it.
How do you give an unattended agent a narrow identity in Fabric? Service-principal access to data agents is in preview. No session showed a pattern.
How does Purview see a custom agent that is built outside Foundry and Copilot Studio?
What are a 'database constitution' and database instructions, and how do skills and plugins work with coding agents? The attendee's notes name them. No slide is held.
What does Copilot Studio cost for each request? The speaker said that the quantity of Copilot credits for each request is not published.
Can you export an ontology, AI instructions and agent definitions to a different platform?
Nothing in this debrief was tested in our own tenant. Each statement is from a speaker, from Microsoft, or from a third party.
claims.caveat: State this on the site.

claims.text: An agent needs three things: context, limits and proof. The 6 threads of this site sort into these 3 groups, plus a reality check on cost and dependency.
claims.caveat: Synthesis by the attendee and the assistant. No speaker used this grouping.

claims.text: Fabric now gives agents context: the ontology in Fabric IQ. The limits and the proof are not finished. OneLake security gives limits and Purview DSPM for AI gives proof, but to join them into one system is the work of the team that builds the agent.
claims.caveat: Synthesis by the attendee and the assistant. The ontology and DSPM for AI for Fabric are in preview (C103, C507). Sources disagree on the label of OneLake security (C312).

claims.text: The announcements at the conference point one way: agents in each layer of Fabric, with one layer for security and governance below them.
claims.caveat: Synthesis by the attendee and the assistant. See C913 for the press quote.
